_🎯 Functional Correctness_ | _🟠 Major_ | _⚡ Quick win_

**Prevent pending initialization from overwriting the selected task mode.**

`Task` starts `initializeTaskMode()` during construction, but `submitUserMessage()` does not wait for it. If the initial `getState()` resolves after `handleModeSwitch(mode, this)` writes `_taskMode`, initialization can restore the prior provider mode. The submitted message then continues with the wrong task mode.

Only initialize `_taskMode` when it is still `undefined`, as `initializeTaskApiConfigName()` already does. Add a regression test that delays `getState()`, submits a mode immediately, then resolves the initial state.

<details>
<summary>Proposed fix</summary>

```diff
 private async initializeTaskMode(provider: ClineProvider): Promise<void> {
   try {
     const state = await provider.getState()
-    this._taskMode = state?.mode || defaultModeSlug
+    if (this._taskMode === undefined) {
+      this._taskMode = state?.mode || defaultModeSlug
+    }
```

💡 Result:

To hide a command from the Command Palette in a VS Code extension, you can use a when clause within the contributes.menus.commandPalette section of your package.json file [1][2][3]. By default, all commands contributed through the contributes.commands section are automatically shown in the Command Palette [1][2][3]. To override this and restrict visibility, you must explicitly define a menu contribution for the commandPalette menu and set a when clause [2][3]. To hide the command entirely, you can set the when clause to "false" [4][5]: { "contributes": { "menus": { "commandPalette": [ { "command": "yourExtension.yourCommandId", "when": "false" } ] } } } Alternatively, if you want the command to be conditionally visible based on specific states, you can use valid context keys or your own custom context keys set via the setContext command [6][7]. For example: { "contributes": { "menus": { "commandPalette": [ { "command": "yourExtension.yourCommandId", "when": "yourExtension.someContextKey" } ] } } } You can manage your custom context keys programmatically in your extension code [6]: vscode.commands.executeCommand('setContext', 'yourExtension.someContextKey', true); Note that there is a distinction between when clauses and enablement clauses [2][3]. A when clause restricts the visibility of the menu item (the entry in the palette), while an enablement clause (defined in the command contribution) determines whether the command itself is executable, which may still result in the command appearing in the palette as a disabled item [2][7]. To remove the item from the palette entirely, the menu's when clause is the appropriate mechanism [2][3].
